title: Key-Based List Reconciler (Minimal DOM Operations)
concept: O(n) Sibling Diffing using Key Maps
problemStatement: Implement `reconcileChildren(oldChildren, newChildren)` that matches old and new list items by `key`. Returns `{ reused: string[], created: string[], deleted: string[] }`.
interviewTrap: Without keys, React falls back to index comparison. Inserting an item at the beginning causes ALL subsequent items to re-render and mutate.

details.name: Identifies reused, created, and deleted items correctly

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: React's list diffing reconciler transforms an old list of children into a new list with minimal DOM mutations. Using a Map keyed by `key`, React matches existing nodes in O(N) time and tracks a `lastPlacedIndex` to determine which nodes only need to be moved versus created or deleted.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Build a hash map of existing children: `existingMap = new Map(oldChildren.map(c => [c.key, c]))`.
Any nodes remaining in `existingMap` were not reused: record `DELETE` operation for each.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: This algorithm in `packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactChildFiber.js` (`mapRemainingChildren` & `placeChild`) solves the tree edit distance problem in O(N) time instead of the theoretical O(N^3) general tree diffing minimum.

complexity.time: O(N + M) linear time where N is old list length and M is new list length.

edgeCasesHandled: Reordering items (e.g., reversing or shifting) produces minimal MOVE operations.
Adding new items produces INSERT operations.
Removing items generates DELETE operations for unvisited keys.

specifications: React Architecture Docs: Reconciliation Diffing Algorithm
verifiedRules: List reconciliation completes in O(N) linear time using key-based mapping.
lastPlacedIndex tracks relative ordering to minimize DOM node relocations.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: How does React's list reconciliation algorithm work in O(N) time? Explain mapRemainingChildren.
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: React executes a two-pass algorithm in `ReactChildFiber.js`: 1) **First Pass**: it walks old and new children in parallel. As long as keys match, it updates fibers in-place. If keys mismatch, the loop breaks. 2) **Second Pass**: React puts all remaining old children into a `Map<key, Fiber>` (`mapRemainingChildren`). It then loops over remaining new children, querying the Map in O(1) time. Nodes found in the Map are reused; nodes not found are created as new; nodes left in the Map after the loop are marked for deletion.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: The definitive algorithmic question for React list reconciliation.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: What is 'lastPlacedIndex' and how does React detect if a DOM node needs to be MOVED?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: `lastPlacedIndex` tracks the highest index in the old list that has been placed in the new list. As React iterates through new children, if a matched old fiber has `oldIndex < lastPlacedIndex`, it means the node originally appeared BEFORE a node that now appears ahead of it, so it must physically MOVE in the DOM (`Placement` flag). If `oldIndex >= lastPlacedIndex`, the relative order is preserved, and `lastPlacedIndex = oldIndex`.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: Differentiates surface-level React users from engineers who have read React's reconciler source code.

realWorldUseCases.description: Reordering cards between columns with minimal DOM reflows by reusing existing fibers via stable item IDs.

howToExplain.opening: React solves list diffing in O(N) linear time using a two-pass reconciliation algorithm with a Map for key lookups and lastPlacedIndex for movement tracking.
keyPoints: Slow-path collects remaining old fibers into a Map keyed by key/index.
lastPlacedIndex detects whether matched nodes need physical DOM relocations.
Unvisited fibers in the Map are flagged for deletion in a single batch.
howToExplain.closingImpression: React's list diffing is an elegant engineering compromise that solves a theoretically O(N^3) tree edit distance problem in linear time.
analogies: Organizing a bookshelf: you slide books over that are already in order, and only physically pick up and relocate the books that were moved to the front.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming reversing an array of 10 items moves all 10 items in the DOM.
commonMistakes.why: Due to lastPlacedIndex mechanics, React leaves the last item in place and moves the other 9 around it, performing N-1 DOM operations.
commonMistakes.correct: Explain that lastPlacedIndex optimizes relative order to minimize physical DOM node re-insertions.

followUpDeepDive.question: Where in React reconciler source is lastPlacedIndex calculated?
followUpDeepDive.answer: In `packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactChildFiber.js` inside the `placeChild(newFiber, lastPlacedIndex, newIndex)` helper function.
